I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I am of opinion that we should do well to confine our labours to four days in the week, and I have reasons for it which I think not inconsiderable. Our people are worn out with their exertions; and the ablest hand among us has but lately left us. There are studies, moreover, which show that the work done in the shorter week is not less than in the longer, and is sometimes greater; and it would not be the least of its advantages, that we should find it the easier to engage new persons.

I am not insensible that the scheme is a dangerous one, and that those whom we serve may be very little disposed to approve it; but I would have us try it for three months, and see what comes of it.

notes.text: A speaker who opens with an opinion in Austen usually shows some confidence in it. This only announces the reasons that follow and adds no new fact.

plan.gist: The opinion, then the weariness and the loss, then the studies and the gain in engaging new people
plan.why: Austen lets a speaker give an opinion and bind its reasons to it in a single connected paragraph, so the argument reads as a train of judgement and not a list.

plan.gist: The admitted danger, then the trial of three months
plan.why: The concession comes before the proposal, so that the proposal arrives last, as the main point of the period, and sounds the more reasonable for it.

faults.quote: “the ablest hand among us has but lately left us”
faults.why: This drops the specific fact that the departing employee was “our best engineer.” “Hand” makes the person a generic worker and loses the professional role, which matters in an argument about staffing and hiring.

faults.quote: “the scheme is a dangerous one”
faults.why: “Risky” is recast as “dangerous,” which is appreciably stronger and makes the speaker’s concession more alarming than the writer’s.

faults.quote: “those whom we serve may be very little disposed to approve it”
faults.why: The original says clients “might not like it.” “Very little disposed to approve” heightens the anticipated opposition and substitutes formal approval for the simpler issue of client preference.

faults.quote: “the ablest hand among us”
faults.why: Though “hand” can mean worker, this phrasing sounds more like generalized labour or domestic service than a natural Austenian equivalent for an engineer in a colleague-facing proposal; it also contributes to the loss of the original’s specificity.

faults.quote: “Clauses balanced in one period ... — cites Northanger Abbey, ch. 1, ¶ 1”
faults.why: The note does not explain how the cited opening of Northanger Abbey specifically supports this claimed syntactic move. It gives no apt parallel phrase or sentence from the source, so the citation is too vague to verify or teach from.

faults.quote: “A speaker who opens with an opinion in Austen usually shows some confidence in it.”
faults.why: This is an unsupported generalization about Austen, and the stated “liberty” is not clearly a liberty requiring defense. “I think” already expresses an opinion; “I have reasons ... not inconsiderable” is permissible tonal commentary, but the note should identify the actual rhetorical expansion and its effect instead.

faults.quote: “Paragraph 2: (no notes)”
faults.why: The second paragraph contains major Austen-like rhetorical changes—especially “I am not insensible,” the intensified “dangerous,” and the concession-before-proposal construction—but provides no source-based explanation or disclosure of the two fidelity shifts.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a credible Austen-flavoured proposal with a sound argumentative order, but it loses the engineer detail and slightly overstates the client and risk objections. Its notes are too thin and do not adequately support their source claim or disclose consequential wording changes.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

When Dana gave up our engagement to dinner, I was not at all vexed by it; and I must confess, in all honesty, that I was relieved. I had dreaded the evening the whole week together, and of that circumstance I was not proud.

I assured her that it was of no consequence, and that we would name another day; though I did not think that we ever should.

notes.after: When Dana gave up our engagement to dinner, I was not at all vexed by it; and I must confess, in all honesty, that I was relieved.

notes.text: A small parenthetical of confession carries the writer's 'Honestly' in the narrator's own manner; it adds no feeling.
notes.after: I must confess, in all honesty,

rows.text: I assured her that it was of no consequence, and that we would name another day; though I did not think that we ever should.

notes.after: I assured her that it was of no consequence, and that we would name another day

notes.text: The writer's 'fine' is the civil phrase of a person soothing another; Austen's word for it is 'of no consequence', which keeps the sense and the politeness.
notes.after: it was of no consequence

lessons: Your draft is three-to-twelve-word sentences in modern speech; Austen would hold the same facts in two long periods, with the main feeling arriving late (“that I was relieved”) and the civil words reported, not quoted. Practise ending a sentence on the private truth that undoes the polite part, as in “though I did not think that we ever should.”

outline.gist: Dana gives up the dinner; the narrator is not at all vexed
she is, honestly, relieved
she had dreaded it all week and is not proud of it
she tells Dana it is of no consequence and another time shall be found
she does not think they ever will

plan.gist: Dana's withdrawal, the narrator's absence of vexation, and her relief, in one period
plan.why: Austen puts the circumstance first in a subordinate clause and lets the feeling arrive late, with the confession as a parenthesis.

plan.gist: The week of dread and the want of pride in it
plan.why: A short balanced period kept for the narrator's judgement of herself, in the abstract noun the matter invites.

plan.gist: What she said to Dana, and what she privately believed
plan.why: Civil speech is reported rather than quoted, and the private doubt is held to the end of the sentence, where it deflates the civility.

faults.quote: I must confess, in all honesty
faults.why: The two confession-markers are redundant, and “in all honesty” has a comparatively modern, generic sound. Austen commonly gets this effect through a single precise concession or a cooler narratorial qualification, rather than stacking sincerity signals.

faults.quote: I had dreaded the evening the whole week together
faults.why: “The whole week together” is an awkward intensifier in this context. It can mean an uninterrupted span of time, but attached to “dreaded” it sounds more like period-flavoured wording than a natural sentence; “all the week” would be cleaner and more idiomatic.

faults.quote: A small parenthetical of confession carries the writer's 'Honestly'
faults.why: The note calls the phrase a “parenthetical,” but it is not functioning as a detachable parenthesis in the sentence; it is an integrated adverbial qualification. The note should identify the actual move more accurately: replacing direct modern emphasis with a formal self-conscious confession.

faults.quote: Your draft is three-to-twelve-word sentences in modern speech
faults.why: This inaccurately describes the draft. Its sentence lengths are not three to twelve words: “I’d been dreading it all week, and I’m not proud of that” is twelve words, while “Honestly, I was relieved” is four. More importantly, length alone does not establish “modern speech.”

faults.quote: Austen would hold the same facts in two long periods
faults.why: The rewrite itself has three sentences, not two periods: the first paragraph contains two sentences and the second contains one. The lesson therefore misstates its own demonstration.

faults.quote: the civil words reported, not quoted
faults.why: The writer already reported the speech indirectly: “I told her it was fine.” This is not a change the rewrite teaches. The useful lesson is instead the substitution of a more ceremonious civil formula (“of no consequence”) and the placement of the private reservation after it.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves all events, feelings, and their order, and its compressed three-sentence structure works well. Its Austen effect is competent but somewhat generalized, while the teaching material contains several factual and analytical inaccuracies that weaken its usefulness.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass at the end of the week that is past, that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto ours. And they had a huge truck, and two little children; and the father seemed a good man, but his sister was somewhat afar off, and drew not near unto us.

And my mother baked cookies for them straightway: for she desired to find out all things concerning them; whence they came, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.

And it came to pass that I learned the father was a lawyer, and that he was single; yea, he was divorced. And my mother had such a look upon her face, and I knew just what she thought: for she had sought for years to give me in marriage.

notes.text: You give the household a mother who is standoffish, and later say the father is single and divorced. Both cannot be so. I made the standoffish woman the father's sister, so the house keeps a second adult and the father may be single and divorced.
notes.after: but his sister was somewhat afar off, and drew not near unto us
at the end of the week that is past

lessons: Your draft is a row of short, flat statements; the Bible would link them with “and” into long sentences, each turn opened plainly, as in “And it came to pass that I learned”. Practise joining facts that belong together and putting the reason after a colon, as in “and I knew just what she thought: for she had sought for years…”.

outline.gist: A new family comes to live next door, with a truck and two little children
The father seems good; the other adult is distant
My mother bakes cookies at once, wishing to learn all about them
The father is a lawyer, single, divorced
My mother's look; I know her thought; she has long tried to marry me off

plan.gist: The family comes, with their goods and children, and the two adults are named
plan.why: The voice opens with the turn of the story and lays the household out in clauses joined by and, so the reader has the whole house before the visit.

plan.gist: The mother's gift and her desire to know
plan.why: The gift and its reason sit in one sentence, the reason following after a colon and the particulars in a list of three, as the voice loves to count.

plan.gist: The father's state, then the look, the knowing, and the reason
plan.why: The discovery lands last with the mother's look, since the matter hits hardest when the thought is told after its cause is seen.

sense.problem: Your second sentence gives the new household a mother: "The mom is kind of standoffish." Your fourth paragraph says the man of that house "is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced." Both cannot be true of the same household as you have told it: either there is a wife and mother next door, or the father is a single man.
sense.resolution: Least change: make the standoffish woman not the wife — e.g. "His sister is kind of standoffish," or "The grandma is kind of standoffish" — so the household still has a second adult and two little kids, and the father can be divorced and single. Do not make her his ex-wife or a woman who merely lives there as a partner; a sister or grandmother keeps every other sentence true, including your mother's hope of a match.
sense.quote: The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

sense.problem: Echo: a household's true state is discovered through a visit and a gift, and a parent'smatchmaking hope turns on the news.
sense.resolution: No biblical scene is truly echoed here; the anecdote is domestic comedy, not the prodigal's return, the Samaritan, Jonah, Ruth, Joseph, or Ecclesiastes. The rewrite should take nothing from those scenes, and should not import their gravity or their phrasing of journey, mercy or mourning. (The one faint likeness — a parent hoping for a child's good match — belongs to no scene of Scripture closely enough to borrow from.)
sense.quote: My mother baked them cookies right away.

rewrite:
Wherefore the town of our habitation ought to shut Main Street unto the cars on the weekends. For to set our cars in the midst of the town is grievous, and the sidewalks thereof are too narrow for the strollers. Behold, other towns have done this; and their shops do better than they did aforetime.

And some of them that have business in the town will murmur, saying that their customers cannot come unto them. But they will grow used unto it. Verily, the most part of the people walk on foot from the garage even now.

Let us therefore try it in this summer.

For to set our cars in the midst of the town is grievous, and the sidewalks thereof are too narrow for the strollers. Behold, other towns have done this; and their shops do better than they did aforetime.

notes.after: Wherefore the town of our habitation ought to shut Main Street unto the cars on the weekends.
the town of our habitation
Behold, other towns have done this

notes.text: Behold calls the hearer's eye to the example; it adds no matter, only the voice's gesture of attention.
notes.after: Behold, other towns have done this

notes.text: Wherefore gives the opening the sound of a charge laid upon a people; the claim itself is the writer's.
notes.after: Wherefore the town of our habitation ought to shut Main Street unto the cars on the weekends.

rows.text: And some of them that have business in the town will murmur, saying that their customers cannot come unto them. But they will grow used unto it. Verily, the most part of the people walk on foot from the garage even now.

notes.text: Verily stands for the writer's 'Honestly', an oath of plain speaking; the voice takes it as the Bible's own way of vouching for a thing.
notes.after: Verily, the most part of the people walk on foot from the garage even now.

rows.text: Let us therefore try it in this summer.

lessons: Your draft gives its points in short, bare sentences; the King James voice joins them with "and", "for" and "wherefore", so each reason leans on the one before. Practise laying clause beside clause ("is grievous, and the sidewalks thereof are too narrow") and opening with a connective, so the argument reads as one road and not as separate stones.

outline.gist: the town ought to close Main Street to cars on weekends
parking is grievous and the sidewalks too narrow for strollers
other towns have done it and their shops do better than ever
some business owners will say customers cannot reach them
they will grow used to it; most people walk from the garage already
let us try it this summer

plan.why: The Bible lays down the thing to be done before the reasons, as a law is given before its cause.

plan.gist: Two reasons and the example of other towns, joined by and
plan.why: Clause laid beside clause gives each fact equal weight, and the example is called forth with behold.

plan.gist: The murmuring of some, then the answer in two short halves
plan.why: The voice sets the complaint and its answer side by side, so the ear hears them weighed.

plan.gist: Let us try it this summer
plan.why: The close is a plain exhortation, as the prophets end.

faults.quote: their shops do better than they did aforetime
faults.why: This weakens “doing better than ever.” “Better than ever” makes a superlative claim over all previous time; “better than they did aforetime” merely compares present performance with some earlier period.

faults.quote: For to set our cars in the midst of the town is grievous
faults.why: This only loosely renders “Parking downtown is a nightmare.” “Grievous” means burdensome or sorrowful and loses the specific practical difficulty and emphatic frustration conveyed by “a nightmare.”

faults.quote: shut Main Street unto the cars
faults.why: “Unto” does not idiomatically express exclusion here. It sounds as though the street is being shut toward the cars, rather than closed against their access. A biblical-sounding construction would need a clearer preposition or recasting.

faults.quote: the sidewalks thereof are too narrow for the strollers
faults.why: “Strollers” is conspicuously modern in its likely intended sense of pushchairs, while in an older register it can also mean people who stroll. The phrase consequently sounds both anachronistic and slightly unclear.

faults.quote: Let us therefore try it in this summer
faults.why: “In this summer” is not idiomatic English and does not sound like natural King James diction. The original’s “this summer” should remain direct, or be recast idiomatically without the intrusive “in.”

faults.quote: Wherefore the town of our habitation ought to shut Main Street unto the cars on the weekends
faults.why: The sentence accumulates biblical-looking markers rather than achieving King James syntax. “Wherefore” has no preceding consequence to refer back to, “town of our habitation” is inflated for “our town,” and “on the weekends” remains conspicuously modern beside the archaisms.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “Wherefore the town of our habitation ought to shut Main Street unto the cars on the weekends.” — cites Ezekiel 44:2
faults.why: Ezekiel 44:2 concerns a gate that “shall be shut” and does not substantiate this composite wording, especially “wherefore,” “unto,” or “town of our habitation.” The citation makes the move sound more textually grounded than it is.

faults.quote: Verily stands for the writer's 'Honestly', an oath of plain speaking
faults.why: “Verily” is an affirmation of truth, not an “oath.” The note’s explanation is inaccurate and does not teach the distinction between an evidentiary assertion and the writer’s conversational emphasis.

faults.quote: Paragraph 3: (no notes)
faults.why: The rewrite changes “this summer” to “in this summer,” a conspicuous and unsuccessful alteration. Even if no liberty was intended, this departure should have been avoided or accounted for.

faults.quote: The Bible lays down the thing to be done before the reasons, as a law is given before its cause.
faults.why: This is an overly broad claim about biblical structure, not a demonstrated feature of the cited or imitated passages. It gives the writer a rule that is too sweeping to use reliably.

faults.quote: opening with a connective
faults.why: The lesson recommends a device that the rewrite mishandles: opening this self-contained proposal with “Wherefore” falsely implies an already stated premise. It does not explain when a connective is warranted, so the transferable advice risks producing more faulty openings.

faults.quote: so the argument reads as one road and not as separate stones
faults.why: This is evocative but generic. Apart from conjunctions, the lesson offers no concrete revision method for preserving emphasis, handling the objection, or retaining a phrase’s exact force, as the lost force of “better than ever” demonstrates.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the argument’s overall sequence, but it weakens a material claim and contains several unidiomatic pseudo-biblical constructions. Its notes and lesson identify some surface devices, yet their textual support and advice are too loose for a teaching tool.

Here's what I think we should do: close Main Street to cars on weekends. Right now, finding a place to leave your car downtown is a nightmare, and the walks along the street are too narrow for parents pushing their babies. Now, some business owners will complain that their customers can't get to them. I understand the worry, but they'll get used to it. And here's the thing: most people walk from where they leave their cars anyway.
